comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
EPIC CLAIMED and extended with a seventh story (2026-09-03). Recording the operator decisions on the ticket itself so they do not live only in the session log (crystal-parodistic-boar / ba7f-f1c0-20e7-4dbc).

## New story: S6 grusome-ecumenical-polarbear (09da-343c-1ee9-480c)

"Fast-fail gate admission above a configurable concurrency cap." Added on operator input that ~10 plan reviews run in parallel routinely, plus code reviews and autodeploy contending for the same volume.

WHY IT IS LOAD-BEARING, not additive: Option A caps each accumulator via a high-water-mark GC, and such a GC assumes evictable data exists. src/rebar/_snapshot/janitor.py documents that it relies on POSIX delete-on-last-close plus touch-on-read mtime recency and deliberately takes NO per-reader lease — a PID+heartbeat lease was spiked and REJECTED as unsound (N readers per entry, PID reuse, crash-stale leases), following Gitaly/Sourcegraph/Bazel/ccache — and it skips entries inside a grace window. So the janitor may UNLINK an in-flight snapshot, but the blocks are not returned until the last reader closes.

Under ~10 concurrent reviews the held bytes are therefore LIVE, not garbage. A cap set below peak concurrent hold cannot be honoured: the GC runs, finds nothing evictable, and the volume fills anyway. That is the same shape as the failure this epic exists to fix — bug 3276 measured prune's reclaimable ceiling at ~1.06 GB against a 29 GB problem.

Without S6, S2-S5's caps are aspirational under exactly the load that causes the incident. S6 therefore BLOCKS S2, S3, S4 and S5 (edges added), and is itself blocked by S0.

DESIGN (operator-specified): one configurable limit shared by plan-review AND completion-verifier, since both create a copy of the repo at a ref and contend for the same disk. At capacity the call FAST-FAILS with a clear "try again later" congestion message rather than queueing, so clients can modulate their own load. Fast-fail over queueing is deliberate — a queued gate still holds its thread and ~739 MB of resident memory while waiting, so a queue converts disk pressure into memory pressure. The rejection must be distinguishable from a gate verdict so an agent does not read congestion as INDETERMINATE or as a failed review.

## Cap values (operator decision)

Derive each cap from measurement as a sensible DEFAULT, and make it settable via a config value — not a hardcoded constant. Grounding available: root working set at the outage was 28G — /var/lib/docker 17G (overlay2 16G across 67 layer dirs), /var/tmp 3.6G, /var/log 1.8G (journal 1.7G) — with ~6.5 GB of that orphaned overlay2 invisible to prune. Note each new config key trips the shrink-only mechanism ratchet and needs an in-tree justification marker naming its ticket, never a baseline edit.

## Tree shape — this lands as ONE STACK

S2-S5 are NOT file-disjoint: all four touch infra/scripts/observability.sh, infra/scripts/compose-up.sh and infra/scripts/install-disk-ceilings.sh. Parallel worktrees are only licensed for genuinely disjoint leaves, so the seven stories land as a single ordered Gerrit stack. The plan-review gate independently reached the same conclusion (advisory P5: "sibling tickets touch the same file(s) with no ordering edge").

## Three gate advisories the implementation must honour

1. Epic AC4 ("existing root/data disk alarms remain present; the cyclopean missing-data fix is not regressed") is covered by NO child story's acceptance criteria. It needs an explicit check in whichever leaf lands last, or its own criterion.
2. S2 and S5 overlap: writable container layers live IN overlay2, so their caps interact and must be designed as one budget rather than two independent ones.
3. S4's /var/tmp cap conflicts with sibling task 3e92 (scowlful-bovine-dragonfly), which documents /var/tmp/rebar-evidence/<ticket>-<stamp>/ as the trap-cleaned evidence location. Capping /var/tmp must not evict evidence mid-investigation.

## Attestation note

The epic's plan-review needed two runs: the first returned INDETERMINATE with zero blocking findings, cause llm-degrade NEEDS_INVESTIGATION (LLM infrastructure, not a plan defect — prior tickets exist for the same condition on completion-verify). The retry PASSED and signed at head_sha ebbcd7a030d6029216127c83fb43c415117af366.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
ADR number and slug reconciled to 0112 across AC1, the 'ADR draft location' note and all 12 file_impact paths. The epic had been stale since the FIRST renumber (0110 -> 0111), not just the second, and the plan-review gate on S0 caught it as a parent/child divergence rather than S0 catching it itself.

S0 (7dfa / livid-blondish-shearwater) is claimed and pushed as Gerrit change 2598. Next is S6 (bounded gate concurrency), which is the precondition for S2-S5: the snapshot janitor reclaims by high-water mark and relies on POSIX delete-on-last-close, so bytes held by an in-flight gate are live rather than garbage, and a cap below peak concurrent hold cannot be honoured by reclamation alone.

Design note carried forward from research: a fast-fail admission seam already exists (review_bot/low_disk.py plus janitor.py's ensure_min_free_space / SnapshotLowDiskError / DEFAULT_MIN_FREE_GIB, which already refuse BEFORE cloning on a free-space floor). S6 should add a concurrency term to that existing seam rather than build a parallel mechanism -- which also keeps it clear of the mechanism-delta ratchet. Separately, REBAR_GATE_TMPDIR already parameterises the snapshot store's base dir, so the dedicated-scratch-volume option is largely config rather than new code.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
S4's two alarms APPLIED, scoped deliberately — and the drift that surfaced them is the epic proving its own thesis.

## What happened

The Terraform Drift workflow, repaired an hour earlier by change 2658 (`fd2b`/`eebc`), ran at 06:34 UTC and FAILED on drift for the first time in days. Its finding:

    aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm.var_tmp_cleanup_not_active   will be created
    aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm.var_tmp_usage_high           will be created
    aws_instance.gerrit                                      will be updated in-place
        user_data  73abb917c5322e67... -> c8bc65ae948d1a...

Those alarms are S4's own, declared when 2659 merged an hour before and never applied. **This is the same shape as S1**, whose volume and alarms were declared and unapplied and invisible for two days because `fmt -check` aborted the run before `plan` could speak (`renowned-corked-hapuku`, `dcc3-75ee-26ce-4840`). The difference is that this time the workflow said so within the hour.

## What I applied, and what I did not

Targeted apply, verified scope first from a worktree pinned at `origin/main` (a stale tree reports a misleading "No changes" — bug `eebc`):

    Plan:  2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy
    Apply: 2 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed

Live and verified:

    rebar-var-tmp-cleanup-not-active   metric var_tmp_cleanup_active   treat_missing_data=breaching  SNS-actioned
    rebar-var-tmp-usage-high           metric var_tmp_used_percent     treat_missing_data=breaching  SNS-actioned

**I did NOT apply the `aws_instance.gerrit` half.** Changing `user_data` on a running EC2 instance requires a STOP/START, and the plan showed `public_ip`/`public_dns` going to `(known after apply)` — so an unscoped apply would take Gerrit down and possibly move its address. Note also that `user_data` only takes effect at boot, so applying it changes nothing operationally until the instance is next started: the stop/start IS the change, not a side effect. That is an operator-timed decision, not a drift-remediation reflex.

## Expect these two to go to ALARM shortly, and that is CORRECT

Both are currently `INSUFFICIENT_DATA` because the host is not yet publishing `var_tmp_cleanup_active` or `var_tmp_used_percent` — S4's `vartmp-cap.sh` and its observability §2h section are merged but not yet deployed to the box. With `treat_missing_data = breaching` they will fire rather than sit silent.

That is the designed dead-man behaviour and should NOT be read as a fault or muted: until autodeploy delivers S4's probe, the `/var/tmp` ceiling genuinely is not in effect, and S4's own reasoning was that a dead timer is the state most likely to be mistaken for a working ceiling. The alarm saying so is the guarantee working, not noise.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
CORRECTION and status on S4's alarms, now that they have data.

Earlier I wrote that the host 'is not yet publishing' S4's metrics and that the alarms would fire purely on missing data. **That was half wrong.** Measured now:

    rebar-var-tmp-cleanup-not-active   ALARM on REAL DATA
        var_tmp_cleanup_active = 0.0 at 06:32, 06:42, 06:47 -- below threshold 1.0
    rebar-var-tmp-usage-high           ALARM on MISSING DATA
        var_tmp_used_percent -- no datapoints received, 3 periods treated as breaching

So the probe is PARTIALLY deployed: `observability.sh` (which autodeploy delivers with the merge) publishes the heartbeat, and the heartbeat is reporting **0 = the cleanup mechanism is not alive**. That is not an artefact of a missing deploy; it is the measurement working and telling the truth.

## What it is telling us, and why it is correct

S4's byte ceiling is installed by `vartmp-cap.sh` via the `compose-up.sh` / `user_data` path — NOT by `observability.sh`. That path requires the `aws_instance.gerrit` update the Terraform Drift run surfaced, which I deliberately did NOT apply because changing `user_data` on a running instance forces a STOP/START (with `public_ip` going to `known after apply`).

So the current state is exactly what the two alarms say:

- the observability half is live and honest;
- the enforcement half is not installed, so `/var/tmp` is **unbounded on the host right now**;
- `var_tmp_used_percent` cannot be measured because there is no cap to measure against.

This is S4's own design working as intended. Its author wrote that `var_tmp_cleanup_active` is alarmed precisely because *'a stale drop-in or dead timer is the state most likely to be mistaken for a working ceiling'*. The alarm is refusing to let exactly that mistake happen.

## The operator decision this surfaces

Getting `/var/tmp` actually bounded requires applying the instance update, which means a scheduled Gerrit stop/start. That is a timing call, not a drift-remediation reflex, and I am not taking it unattended: the earlier docker restart was a ~20-second container bounce, whereas this stops and starts the EC2 instance and may move its public address.

Until it is applied, treat both alarms as ACCURATE rather than noisy, and do not mute them — the condition they report is real.

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
Disk measurement, 2026-09-05 ~08:30 UTC — evidence for the remaining caps (S3/S4/S5).

Correcting my own probe first: my initial CloudWatch query returned "no datapoints" for every metric and I nearly read that as a dead probe. It was my error twice over — the namespace is lowercase `rebar/host` (I queried `Rebar/Host`; namespaces are case-sensitive), and the returned timestamps carry a `-07:00` offset, so my hour-slice was reading local-offset rather than UTC. With both corrected, five of six metrics ARE publishing currently. Only `var_tmp_used_percent` is genuinely absent.

Measured, namespace `rebar/host`:

- `docker_unaccounted_bytes` — 2.03 GB (08:19 UTC) -> 2.86 -> 3.02 -> 3.02 -> **3.79 GB (08:29 UTC)**. Threshold is 2 GiB. The scheduled `systemctl restart docker` at 05:23 UTC had brought this to 1.42 GB, so this is ~2.4 GB of regrowth in roughly three hours, and it is still climbing.
- `docker_buildkit_cache_used_percent` — 99-100% sustained across the whole window, against the 5 GiB BuildKit budget.

The pair is the informative part. BuildKit sitting pinned at ~100% of its budget is the cap DOING its job — that number is bounded because `builder.gc` is in effect (confirmed earlier by ordering: daemon.json written 01:01 UTC, dockerd ActiveEnterTimestamp 05:23:33 UTC). The unaccounted bytes are the part NOT under any cap, and they are the ones growing. So the storage growth is escaping through the space the container-layer and scratch caps (S3/S5) are meant to close, not through the BuildKit budget already installed by S0/S6.

Two alarm states here are known-pending and are NOT new findings:
- `var_tmp_cleanup_active` = 0 across all 33 datapoints. Genuine breach, expected: S4's terraform alarms were applied, but the host-side cleanup unit ships in `user_data`, and the `aws_instance.gerrit` update that installs it was deliberately declined tonight because it requires a Gerrit stop/start. `var_tmp_used_percent` publishing nothing has the same single cause.
- `gate_scratch_mounted` = 0 across all 33 datapoints. This is dcc3 — the volume is attached but raw/unmounted, and mounting it hides ~9.3 GB of live data, so it needs a quiet window.

Not filing a bug for the docker regrowth: it is this epic's subject, and a separate ticket would duplicate S3/S5 rather than add anything. Recording it here as a measured baseline the remaining stories can be judged against.

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
Epic-level consolidation: TWO of this epic's caps are gated on the same host reboot, and that is an operator decision rather than an implementation gap.

S4 (`/var/tmp`) and S5 (container writable layers) hit the same constraint independently, from opposite directions, and both concluded the same thing: the enforcement mechanism they wanted needs an XFS project quota on the filesystem backing the resource, that filesystem is ROOT in both cases, and XFS reads quota options at MOUNT time and refuses them on a remount. So each needs `rootflags=pquota` and a reboot before its hard ceiling can exist at all. S5's report also records the daemon refusing it in one line — `--storage-opt is supported only for overlay over xfs with 'pquota' mount option` — which is the mechanism confirming the constraint rather than an inference about it.

What that means for the epic's claim. All seven stories now have changes pushed, so the epic is complete as AUTHORED. But the ceiling it promises is not uniformly a bound in production today:

- Bounded and in service: the BuildKit budget (S0/S6). Measured pinned at 99-100% of its 5 GiB share, which is the cap working — the number is bounded because something bounds it.
- Bounded for the debris it can reach, NOT for the live set: S5's reaper. Its own report is explicit that it "cannot reclaim a RUNNING container's writable layer at all", so for the live compose set it ships measurement and an alarm rather than a bound, with a stated escape rate of ~7.2 MB/s sustained net fill against a 125 MB/s volume baseline.
- Not in service pending the reboot: S4's `/var/tmp` hard quota, and S5's per-container quota.

Two honesty notes, because the difference matters when someone later asks whether this epic delivered.

First, both stories published an unalarmed truth metric rather than asserting the cap was live — `container_quota_enforceable` publishes 0 until the reboot, and S4's `var_tmp_hard_quota_in_effect` does the equivalent. That is the right shape: the gap is VISIBLE rather than silent, which is exactly the failure mode this epic exists to close. `var_tmp_cleanup_active` reading 0 across all 33 samples tonight is that design working as intended, not a defect.

Second, the reboot is genuinely the operator's call and I am not scheduling it. Rebooting the production Gerrit host takes Gerrit, the MCP server, and the review-bot down together, and the epic's remaining benefit does not justify an unattended overnight reboot. Recording it here so the decision is visible with its cost rather than discovered later as an unexplained "the cap does not work".

Live context for that decision, measured this tick: root filesystem is at 70% and climbing (48.6% -> 70% over roughly 12 hours). The docker restart at 05:23 UTC produced a ~1-point dip and did not change the slope. A diagnosis of what is actually producing the growth is in flight; until it reports, the reboot's urgency is unknown, and I would rather the operator decide against a named producer than against a trend line.

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
Correction to my disk-measurement comment above.

I cited `docker_unaccounted_bytes` (2.03 -> 3.79 GB in 40 minutes) as showing that "the storage growth is escaping through the space the container-layer and scratch caps close, not through the BuildKit budget already installed by S0/S6". I withdraw that inference.

There is an open p2 bug on that metric — `regretful-enormous-horsefly` — measured on this host today. `docker_unaccounted_bytes` differences an ALLOCATED-BLOCKS `du -sx --block-size=1 /var/lib/docker` against APPARENT-size `docker system df` rows. Across ~1.88M files on 4 KiB xfs blocks that inflates the minuend ~12.4%, and the inflation scales with the tree. Measured split of a 2,685,139,712-byte residue: 1,501,924,837 bytes (56%) is xfs block-allocation overhead, only 1,183,214,875 bytes (44%) is real un-ledgered content. So most of the level, and plausibly most of the delta, is an artifact rather than bytes.

What that changes for this epic's assessment, precisely:

- The claim that growth is escaping specifically through the writable-layer/scratch gap is NOT supported by the evidence I gave for it. It may still be true — S5's own report is explicit that a running container's writable layer is unbounded and unreclaimable — but I had not measured it, and the number I used cannot establish it.
- The claim that the BuildKit cap IS working still stands, and does not depend on the defective metric: `docker_buildkit_cache_used_percent` is a direct ratio against its own budget, pinned at 99-100%, which is a bound holding rather than a difference of incommensurable units.
- The root-filesystem trajectory (48.6% -> 70%) stands — it is a direct filesystem measurement.

So the epic's honest position is narrower than I stated: root is definitely filling, the BuildKit cap is definitely holding, and the ATTRIBUTION of the remaining growth is still open. A diagnosis is in flight and I have passed the same correction to it, along with that bug's genuinely useful finding — 20 `overlay2` directories referenced by neither cache-id nor mount-id, totalling 1,012,375,552 bytes, though with 2026-09-02 mtimes, so static and not the current producer.

None of this changes the reboot note above, which rests on S4's and S5's own mechanism findings rather than on any metric.

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
## Live root-disk diagnosis, 2026-09-05 09:15-09:55 UTC (read-only SSM probes, host i-00880b2c7f13527c5)

Diagnosis only — no host state was mutated. Everything below marked MEASURED is a direct
probe result; anything marked INFERRED is not.

### Headline: root is not on a monotonic climb. It is a ~2 GB SAWTOOTH.

MEASURED `df -k /` series (used KB, then Use%):

```
09:15:11  42,176,944  68%
09:17:16  42,176,944  68%
09:19:54  42,177,348  68%
09:27:57  42,396,420  68%
09:33:53  44,359,964  71%   <-- +2.08 GB vs 09:19
09:36:26  44,158,704  71%
09:37:26  43,992,476  71%
09:38:26  42,412,096  68%   <-- -1.58 GB in ONE minute
09:39:26  42,493,052  68%
09:40:26  42,926,260  69%
```

Between 09:15 and 09:20 root grew **404 KB in 2.6 minutes** — essentially flat. Then it rose
2.08 GB and gave 1.58 GB straight back. The "+1.69 pts/hr sustained" reading is an artifact of
sampling a sawtooth; the amplitude is ~2 GB (~3.3 points) and the period is tens of minutes.
This matches the 08:44 -> 09:14 partial reversal in the 15-minute series.

### The producer: `rebar-autodeploy.timer` build+recreate cycles

MEASURED, `systemctl cat rebar-autodeploy.timer`:

```
OnBootSec=2min
OnUnitActiveSec=2min
```

The timer polls every 2 minutes and rebuilds whenever `main` advances. MEASURED from
`journalctl -u rebar-autodeploy`, `main` advanced seven times in the probe window:
`070c54e6 -> 1f1ecea0 -> a33333b8 -> c0199203 -> c4e43e3f -> cf9c3daf -> 8629e387`, with
`mcp` or `review-bot` image builds at 06:19, 06:32, 06:33, 07:40, 08:07, 08:30, 09:10, 09:13
— roughly one build every 20-25 minutes.

### Where the oscillating bytes live: container writable layers in overlay2

MEASURED per-container `GraphDriver.Data.UpperDir` sizes at 09:33:53 (peak of the sawtooth):

| Container | State | Started | UpperDir size |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rebar-mcp-adfc5285fad6-8092` | running | 09:11:25 | **2,097,656 KB (2.10 GB)** |
| `rebar-mcp-9d5a7278c892-8093` | **exited** | 08:30:57 | **1,858,500 KB (1.86 GB)** |
| `compose-gerrit-1` | running | 05:23:32 | 430,956 KB (431 MB) |
| `compose-review-bot-1` | running | 08:29:47 | 16 KB |
| `compose-opcert-1` | running | 05:23:32 | 0 KB |

So **3.96 GB sat in two blue-green MCP writable layers simultaneously**, one of them exited and
still resident. The running MCP container accumulated **2.10 GB in ~22 minutes**.

Cross-check that this IS the oscillating mass — MEASURED `du -xsk /var/lib/docker/overlay2`:

```
09:17:16  12,338,996 KB
09:33:53  13,852,180 KB   (+1.51 GB)
~09:45    12,167,268 KB   (-1.69 GB)
```

The 1.69 GB overlay2 drop matches the 1.58 GB df drop at 09:38. The sawtooth is
**overlay2 container writable layers**, not build cache and not anything outside docker.

INFERRED (not directly measured): the ~2 GB inside each `rebar-mcp` writable layer is the
tickets-store clone that `reviewbot-ensure-tickets.sh` performs at container start
(`git clone --single-branch --branch tickets`). I did not walk the diff dir to confirm its
contents.

### Aggravating factor: 21-minute container recreates hold BOTH layers

MEASURED:

```
08:08:15  Container compose-review-bot-1  Recreate
08:29:47  Container compose-review-bot-1  Recreated   (21m32s)
09:13:24  Container compose-review-bot-1  Recreate
09:34:24  Container compose-review-bot-1  Recreated   (21m00s)
```

For 21 minutes on every redeploy the old and new container layers coexist on root. That is the
rising half of the sawtooth, and the fall is the old container finally being reaped.

### The reclaim is reporting success while freeing nothing

MEASURED `prune_docker_caches` lines from the same journal, in order:

```
06:13:50  freed=434,236 kB
06:20:05  freed=4 kB
06:32:54  freed=310,048 kB
06:33:33  freed=190,040 kB
07:40:44  freed=187,076 kB
08:29:57  freed=564 kB
08:31:22  freed=348,456 kB
09:12:39  freed=125,564 kB
09:34:40  freed=988 kB
```

Median ~190 MB against a ~2 GB swing; three of nine runs freed under 1 MB and still logged as a
normal outcome. This is the pattern already captured on `taurine-smiling-hamadryad`
("reports success without measuring effect"), still live.

### The BuildKit budget is being EXCEEDED, not merely pinned

MEASURED `docker system df`:

```
Images         5   4   3.081GB   957.7MB (31%)
Containers     4   4   1.369GB   0B (0%)
Local Volumes 11   1   988.7MB   1.207MB (0%)
Build Cache  104   0   5.875GB   5.875GB
```

`daemon.json` sets `builder.gc.maxUsedSpace = 5368709120` (5.00 GiB). Build cache is at
**5.875 GB across 104 entries, 0 active, 100% reclaimable** — i.e. ~0.9 GB OVER budget with GC
lagging the build cadence. The `docker_buildkit_cache_used_percent` metric reading "99-100%" is
therefore under-reporting an overshoot, not showing a cap holding at its limit.

### Ruled out, with numbers

- **Deleted-but-open files** — MEASURED total across every `/proc/*/fd`: `deleted_open_bytes=2,097,152` (2 MB). Not the story.
- **`/tmp`** — MEASURED as **tmpfs**, 3.8 G size, **100 KB used**. Host-side gate scratch under `/tmp` costs RAM, not root disk. (Container-internal `/tmp` is a different matter — that IS the overlay2 upper dir above.)
- **`/var/tmp`** — MEASURED 3,751,848 KB (3.75 GB), but 3.75 GB of it is two stale dirs `rebar-review-rehearsal.9eL926` (1.88 GB) and `rebar-review-rehearsal.e3gHec` (1.87 GB), both **mtime 2026-08-27** — nine days old, static. Dead weight, not a producer.
- **journald** — MEASURED `/var/log/journal` 1,795,632 KB (1.80 GB), `/var/log` total 1.93 GB. Flat, bounded, consistent with the 57% metric.
- **`/var/gerrit`** — separate volume `nvme1n1`, MEASURED 9.2 G used of 49.9 G (18%). Not root.

### Confirmed: the gate-scratch volume never entered service

MEASURED: `lsblk` shows `nvme2n1  50G` with **no fstype and no mountpoint**, and
`file -s /dev/nvme2n1` returns `/dev/nvme2n1: data` — raw, unformatted. This independently
confirms `renowned-corked-hapuku` and `findable-sure-lynx`. Because host `/tmp` is tmpfs, the
practical consequence today is that gate scratch lands in **RAM**, not on root — a different
failure mode than `1ef8` described, and worth noting since `kswapd0` was MEASURED at 3.4% CPU
with `kcompactd0` active, i.e. the host is already under memory pressure.

### An unexplained ~21 GB, which is NOT the grower

MEASURED subtree totals (~09:45):

```
/var/lib/docker   13,227,224 KB   13.23 GB
/var/tmp           3,751,848 KB    3.75 GB
/var/log           1,927,132 KB    1.93 GB
/usr               1,952,540 KB    1.95 GB
/var/cache           156,916 KB    0.16 GB
/opt + /root + /etc + /boot          0.22 GB
                                 ---------
                                   21.24 GB
```

`df` reports **42.4-42.9 GB used** over the same period. **~21 GB is unaccounted.** I could not
close this read-only. `du -x /` does not complete — it timed out at 400 s having reached only
`/local`, `/etc`, `/boot`; the root fs carries **2,343,321 used inodes**.

Leading hypothesis, INFERRED and untested: files **shadowed under mount points** — written to
`/var/gerrit`, to the nine `/var/lib/docker/volumes/*/_data` bind targets, or to `/tmp` before
their filesystems were mounted over them. Both `du -x` and `find -xdev` stop at a mountpoint, so
shadowed content is invisible to every read-only probe I have. Confirming it requires a
mutation (see below).

Note also that `find / -xdev -type f -printf '%b'` sums are **hardlink-inflated** and must not
be compared against `du`: the aggregation returned 59.92 GB for `/var/lib` where `du` says
13.23 GB, a ~4.5x amplification from overlay2 image-layer hardlinks. This is the same
apparent-vs-allocated class of error as `regretful-enormous-horsefly`.

### Is this epic 6202's subject?

**Yes, squarely** — it is Defect 1, "root-volume consumers grow without a bounded ceiling", and
it lands on two children specifically:

- **S5 `francium-written-squid` (in_progress)** — writable container layers. The 3.96 GB
  blue-green MCP pair is exactly this, and it is the dominant term. Per the S5 finding that
  `--storage-opt size=` needs XFS `pquota` and a reboot, running layers are unbounded today.
- **S2 `geode-joking-cockatiel` (closed)** — the BuildKit cap is measurably **over** its 5 GiB
  budget at 5.875 GB with 0 active entries. Worth reopening or filing as a regression.

I did NOT file a new bug. Nothing here needs one; the mechanism is 6202's and the two specific
gaps belong on S5 and S2.

### Mutations that would help — NOT run, operator decides

1. **`docker container prune -f`** (or removing the exited `rebar-mcp-9d5a7278c892-8093`).
   Would reclaim the MEASURED **1.86 GB** exited MCP writable layer. Blast radius: destroys the
   exited container's filesystem and any forensic evidence in it; removes ALL exited containers,
   not just this one. Does not touch running containers. Reversible only from image rebuild.
2. **`docker builder prune -f`.** Would reclaim the MEASURED **5.875 GB** of build cache (0
   entries active, 100% reclaimable). Blast radius: the next autodeploy build loses all layer
   caching, so one build runs cold — minutes slower, and during it root rises again. No data
   loss.
3. **Removing the two stale `/var/tmp/rebar-review-rehearsal.*` dirs.** Would reclaim a MEASURED
   **3.75 GB**. Blast radius: nine-day-old rehearsal artifacts; verify nothing references them
   first. This is the cleanest single reclaim available.
4. **`mount --bind / /mnt/root-view` (read-only diagnostic).** The only way to see shadowed
   content and settle the ~21 GB. Blast radius: adds a mount entry; no data is modified;
   `umount` reverses it. Still a mutation, so I did not run it.

None of these change the sawtooth. The sawtooth is bounded and self-reclaiming; the real risk is
that its ~2 GB peak rides on top of a ~21 GB baseline nobody can currently attribute.

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
Correction, and it is the one that matters most for judging whether this epic delivered: **the BuildKit cap is NOT holding.** I asserted twice above that it was, and I was wrong in a way that inverted the evidence.

**What I claimed.** In two comments I wrote that "the BuildKit cap IS working — the number is bounded because something bounds it", citing `docker_buildkit_cache_used_percent` pinned at 99-100% as positive evidence. I even used it as the contrast case against the defective `docker_unaccounted_bytes`, on the grounds that a direct ratio against a known budget could not mislead the way a difference of incommensurable units could.

**What is actually true.** Measured on the host via `docker system df`:

    Build Cache   5.875 GB   104 entries   0 active

against `builder.gc.maxUsedSpace` = 5.00 GiB = 5.368 GB. The true ratio is **~109%**. The cache is roughly 0.5 GB PAST its budget, with zero active entries — so this is retained reclaimable cache, not work in progress.

**Why the metric said 100.** `pct_of_cap` in `infra/scripts/observability.sh:304-309` clamps: `[ "$pct" -gt 100 ] && pct=100`. The metric cannot express an overshoot. "Exactly at cap" and "over cap" are the same published number, so a cap breach renders as a healthy-looking pinned ceiling. I have filed that separately as **`undefiled-revivable-gemsbok`** (`b380-3dfc-99fc-4a0e`, p2), linked `discovered_from` this epic; it affects three metrics — `docker_storage_used_percent`, `docker_buildkit_cache_used_percent` and `journal_used_percent` — all of which are cap-compliance gauges that go blind exactly when their cap fails.

**The compounding error was mine, not just the metric's.** `rebar-docker-buildkit-cache-high` (threshold 85, GreaterThanThreshold) has been in ALARM this whole time and I discounted it as "the cap doing its job". A firing alarm was telling me the truth and I read the clamped ceiling underneath it as reassurance. That is worth recording because it is the failure mode the clamp creates: it does not merely lose precision, it converts an alarm into its opposite.

**What this does to the epic's honest position.** My earlier three-way summary needs revising:

- BuildKit budget (S0/S6): **NOT bounded in production today.** 9% over, 104 retained entries, 0 active. Whether that is a `builder.gc` configuration problem, a reclamation that is not running, or a best-effort target being treated as a hard wall is not established — `builder.gc.maxUsedSpace` is documented as best-effort, so exceeding it is not by itself proof of a defect, but it IS proof that the epic cannot claim a bound here.
- S5's reaper: bounds exited containers only, and its own report says it cannot touch a running container's writable layer. A measured **1.86 GB** currently sits in an EXITED `rebar-mcp-9d5a7278c892-8093` layer that the reaper would reclaim, so it has real work waiting for it.
- S4 `/var/tmp` and S5's per-container quota: still blocked on the `rootflags=pquota` reboot.

So of the epic's caps, one is unbounded-and-was-reported-as-bounded, one is partial by design, and two await a reboot. That is a materially weaker position than I recorded earlier tonight, and it is weaker because I mis-read the evidence, not because anything regressed in the last hour.

Root-cause diagnosis of the growth itself is on the separate comment thread; the short version is that root is a ~2 GB SAWTOOTH driven by `rebar-autodeploy.timer` rebuilding on every `main` advance with 21-minute container recreates, not the monotonic climb I originally described.

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
All seven children are now CLOSED (S0-S6). This epic still cannot close, and the gap is worth stating precisely because "every child is closed" is exactly the signal that invites a premature epic close.

The children assert CODE. This epic's own acceptance criteria assert the PRODUCTION OUTCOME. Those are different claims, and right now three of the seven are false on the live host.

**AC2 — FALSE.** *"Dedicated gate-scratch EBS volume exists, IS MOUNTED at a documented path, IS USED by gate snapshots and review clone tempdirs, and has its own disk alarm."* The volume exists and the alarm exists; the mount does not. Confirmed directly on the host this morning: `nvme2n1`, 50G, **no fstype**, `file -s` reports `data` — i.e. raw, never formatted. `gate_scratch_mounted` publishes 0 on every sample. This is ticket `dcc3`, and it is the S1 deliverable that never entered service. Until it mounts, the "is used by" half is false too — gate scratch is still landing on root, which is the condition this epic was created to end.

**AC3 — FALSE for at least one named accumulator.** *"Each named root accumulator has an ENFORCED cap and its own CloudWatch alarm at/near cap."* The alarms all exist. The enforcement does not, in three places:
- BuildKit cache measured at **5.875 GB against a 5.00 GiB (5.368 GB) budget** — roughly 9% over, 104 retained entries, 0 active. Not enforced.
- `/var/tmp` hard quota (S4) and the per-container writable-layer quota (S5) both need XFS `pquota` on the ROOT filesystem, which requires `rootflags=pquota` and a REBOOT. Neither is in force.
- S5's reaper bounds EXITED containers only and its own report states it cannot reclaim a RUNNING container's writable layer at all — so for the live compose set it is measurement plus an alarm, not a cap.

**AC5 — UNVERIFIED.** *"`scowlful-bovine-dragonfly` is linked as the carried-over `/var/gerrit` sibling and is resolved or explicitly dispositioned BEFORE EPIC CLOSE."* I have not checked its state; whoever closes this must, since the criterion names epic close explicitly.

The other four (ADR landed, existing alarms not regressed, runbooks, portability) I believe hold on the children's evidence, but I have not re-verified them at epic level and am not ticking anything.

**Why I am flagging this rather than just leaving it open.** Two of these three failures are the same defect class this epic exists to fix, recurring one level up: a deliverable that is built, merged, closed, and NOT IN SERVICE. `dcc3` is S1's; `renowned-corked-hapuku` records the same shape. An epic closed on child-count would convert "we shipped the code" into "the host has a bounded ceiling", which is precisely the claim that is not true.

**What remains, concretely:** mount the gate-scratch volume (needs a quiet window — mounting hides ~9.3 GB of live data under the mount point); decide on the `rootflags=pquota` reboot, which takes Gerrit, the MCP server and the review-bot down together and is an operator call I am not making; and establish whether the BuildKit overshoot is a misconfiguration or `builder.gc.maxUsedSpace` behaving as the best-effort target it is documented to be. Note the measurement that revealed the overshoot was itself hidden by a clamped metric — `undefiled-revivable-gemsbok`, linked `discovered_from` here.

Not closing. Not ticking. Recording so the next reader does not mistake a complete child list for a delivered outcome.

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
Correcting a claim I made in my own correction above. The BuildKit overshoot was real; my account of how the alarm behaved was not.

**What I wrote earlier:** that `rebar-docker-buildkit-cache-high` "has been in ALARM this whole time and I discounted it as the cap doing its job. A firing alarm was telling me the truth and I read the clamped ceiling underneath it as reassurance." I offered that as the lesson — that a clamped metric converts an alarm into its opposite.

**What is actually true.** I read the alarm's own state, and it did not fire on the value:

    state: ALARM   StateUpdatedTimestamp: 2026-09-04T17:51:49
    eval=3  datapoints_to_alarm=2  period=300  threshold=85  op=GreaterThanThreshold
    treat_missing_data=breaching
    StateReason: "no datapoints were received for 3 periods and 3 missing
                  datapoints were treated as [Breaching]"

It entered ALARM on **missing data**, roughly ten and a half hours before I looked at it, and has not left. It was never reporting the overshoot. The overshoot and the alarm coexisted by coincidence.

So the lesson I drew was wrong in an instructive direction: I built a tidy story — "the alarm was right, the clamp made me misread it" — that was more satisfying than the evidence supported, and I did it while in the middle of correcting a different overstatement. The clamp finding (`undefiled-revivable-gemsbok`) stands on its own measurement: cache at 5.875 GB against a 5.00 GiB budget, metric publishing 100. What does not stand is my claim that the alarm surface was signalling it.

**And the alarm is worse than merely uninformative — it cannot clear.** `docker_buildkit_cache_used_percent` has ONE datapoint in the last 40 minutes (10:54Z = 0, correctly reflecting the pruned cache). With `datapoints_to_alarm=2` of `evaluation_periods=3` at a 300s period and `treat_missing_data=breaching`, a metric publishing less than twice per fifteen minutes keeps two "breaching" gaps in every evaluation window permanently. So this alarm will stay red regardless of the cache's actual size. It is not stuck by a fault; it is structurally unclearable at the current publish cadence.

**What that means for AC3 here.** It does not change the verdict — AC3 ("each named root accumulator has an ENFORCED cap and its own CloudWatch alarm at/near cap") is still not met — but it changes WHY. I previously implied the alarm half was working and only enforcement was missing. In fact this accumulator's alarm is presently incapable of distinguishing a bounded cache from an unbounded one, so both halves of the criterion fail for it. Recorded on `illbred-sour-alpaca`, which owns the alarm mechanism.

Post-prune state for the record: cache 0B, `docker_buildkit_cache_used_percent` 0, root 65-66% and holding.

compiled_state.description:
# Bounded disk-ceiling architecture for the Gerrit host

## Context
Discovered from `cyclopean-bloodshot-hoatzin` (`3276-2f81-8c75-4ddd`), the 2026-09-02 root-volume outage that took Gerrit offline for ~5h. Defect 2 from that incident (disk alarms self-cleared when metrics stopped because `treat_missing_data=notBreaching`) stays on that bug and was fixed/landed/applied live. This epic is Defect 1: root-volume consumers grow without a bounded ceiling.

Operator-approved design — firm standing intent, do not re-litigate:

1. **Option A: per-accumulator HARD SIZE CAPS via native GC/retention.** Each disk consumer gets a hard upper bound enforced by its own native garbage-collection or retention mechanism. Consumers to cap: Docker overlay2/image layers + build cache (BuildKit/Docker GC policy with `maxUsedSpace` / `--keep-storage` style limits), `/var/tmp` (tmpfiles cleanup plus a real size/quota mechanism where required), journald (`SystemMaxUse`), and writable container layers (runtime storage quota where supportable, or bounded periodic reaping of exited containers). **Hard operator constraint:** every capped generator must have its own CloudWatch alarm at/near its cap, so capacity visibility names the saturated generator rather than only saying "root disk high".
2. **Option C: separate EBS volume for code-review scratch.** Gate scratch/clones/snapshots currently share root via system temp (e.g. `/tmp/rebar-gate-snapshots`). Move this workload to a dedicated, independently sized/quota'd gp3 EBS volume mounted at a documented path, and configure gate temp/snapshot code so review work can never fill the OS/root disk.
3. **Sibling carried from cyclopean AC5:** fold in `scowlful-bovine-dragonfly` (`3e92-b7f4-dede-4c17`), the `/var/gerrit` data-volume prevention/runbook task, by linking it into this epic rather than duplicating it.

The root volume was grown 30→60 GiB during recovery and should stay 60 GiB, but that is headroom only, not the fix: an unbounded generator can fill 60 GiB as readily as 30 GiB.

## Scope
This epic scaffolds and later implements the approved architecture only. Defect 2 alarm-missing-data remediation remains on `cyclopean-bloodshot-hoatzin`. The full ADR draft is captured in child S0 to keep this epic below the 8,000-character plan-review admission cap; no ADR file is created by this scaffold-only work.

## Research grounding
- Current Terraform owns a single EC2 host plus `/var/gerrit` data EBS volume: `infra/terraform/main.tf:27-35`, `:42-64`, `:83-87`; size variables are in `infra/terraform/variables.tf:13-23`.
- `infra/terraform/user_data.sh:20-70` is the existing attach/mount pattern: resolve Nitro NVMe device by EBS volume id, format idempotently, mount by UUID in `/etc/fstab`.
- `infra/scripts/compose-up.sh:21-31` and `:82-99` create Docker bind volumes under `/var/gerrit/site`; current review-bot compose has no tmp/scratch mount and notes `REBAR_GATE_TMPDIR` is unset (`infra/compose/docker-compose.yml:233-245`).
- Snapshot store and clone locations: `src/rebar/_snapshot/repo_snapshot.py:149-163` uses `REBAR_GATE_TMPDIR` else `tempfile.gettempdir()` and creates `rebar-gate-snapshots`; `src/rebar/review_bot/voter.py:381` clones into `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="reviewbot-")`; `src/rebar/review_bot/low_disk.py:69` checks free space on `tempfile.gettempdir()`.
- Observability/alarm seams: `infra/scripts/observability.sh:72-90` publishes current data/root disk metrics; root alarm is `infra/terraform/monitoring_autodeploy.tf:207-239`; data alarm is `infra/terraform/monitoring.tf:217-244`.
- Existing reactive reclaimers are in `infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh:132-140`, `:367-384`, and `:410-445`; runbook coverage is `infra/runbooks/review-bot-ops.md:494-606` and provisioning order is `infra/runbooks/provision-restore.md:98-138`.
- Prior incident tickets found: `resting-feudalist-screamer` (`2731`), `masonic-abeyant-stagbeetle` (`3a52`), `besotted-witty-murrelet` (`e4f3`), `preodorous-temporary-piglet` (`3cef`), current `cyclopean-bloodshot-hoatzin` (`3276`), plus data-volume sibling `wakeful-ordinary-chicken` (`5a05`).

## ADR draft location
S0 `livid-blondish-shearwater` contains the full ADR draft to land later as `docs/adr/0112-on-box-disk-ceiling-architecture.md` plus `docs/adr/.numbers/0112`, matching `docs/adr/README.md` and recent ADR format. Related accepted ADRs to cite: ADR 0005, ADR 0012, ADR 0069/0077, and ADR 0104.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] ADR 0112 is finalized and landed in `docs/adr/` with number marker and index update if required by repo convention.
- [ ] Dedicated gate-scratch EBS volume exists, is mounted at a documented path, is used by gate snapshots and review clone tempdirs, and has its own disk alarm.
- [ ] Each named root accumulator has an enforced cap and its own CloudWatch alarm at/near cap.
- [ ] Existing root/data disk alarms remain present; the cyclopean missing-data fix is not regressed.
- [ ] `scowlful-bovine-dragonfly` is linked as the carried-over `/var/gerrit` sibling and is resolved or explicitly dispositioned before epic close.
- [ ] Runbooks document steady-state ceilings, per-generator alarms, and emergency remediation.
- [ ] Portability criterion: implementation is Terraform + host Docker/systemd config + host metrics, with local/scripted validation; it does not depend on any single CI provider trigger.

## ADR number/slug corrected 0110 -> 0112 (2026-09-03)

This epic's AC1, its "ADR draft location" note and its `file_impact` originally named
`docs/adr/0110-gerrit-disk-ceiling-architecture.md` / `.numbers/0110`. That number and slug are
both superseded; the deliverable is `docs/adr/0112-on-box-disk-ceiling-architecture.md` /
`.numbers/0112`. Parent and child now name the same deliverable.

**Why the number moved twice.** The original plan asserted "the highest current number is 0109"
and selected 0110 — that research was already stale: `docs/adr/0110-change-shape-advisory-not-blocking.md`
and its marker had landed in commit 8f19115cf2fb. S0 was renumbered to 0111, and then 0111 was
taken too, by in-flight Gerrit change 2592 (`docs/adr/0111-no-internal-only-compatibility-shims.md`
plus `.numbers/0111`), which was further along. 0112 is the next free number: `.numbers/` on
`origin/main` holds 0091-0110, change 2592 holds 0111, and no other in-flight change (2593-2597)
touches `docs/adr/` at all.

**Why this keeps happening.** `scripts/check_adr_numbers.py` asserts a bijection between
`.numbers/` markers and ADR files, so a collision is caught — but only at gate time, and the
reservation marker is only created when the ADR is *authored*. Two agents drafting concurrently
will therefore keep colliding, and a plan that reads the highest number at planning time is stale
by the time it lands. Worth a mechanism ticket if it recurs a third time.

**The slug also changed, and the wording is load-bearing.** `docs/adr/README.md` is GENERATED by
`scripts/gen_adr_index.py` (it carries a do-not-edit-by-hand marker) and that script buckets ADRs
into sections by keyword-matching the slug. `on-box` files it under **Infra & deploy**, alongside
0012, 0079 and 0104 — the ADRs it cites. A slug containing `gerrit` mis-files it, and the
"Reconciler & Jira sync" group claims the keyword `bound`, so `bounded-disk-ceiling-...` would
mis-file too. Regenerate README; never hand-edit it.
